name: Wendy Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead eight people in the supply planning unit of a large company, though I'm only 27. I earned an MBA, and most mornings start with a late order report, a quick AI draft, and a call where somebody has to own the fix. I like the moment we prevent a customer delay; I hate having my pay called a growth opportunity.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What follows you home from that day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The MBA loan and rent. I live alone, and my savings would cover less than a month, so a calm meeting at work doesn't mean a calm evening at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my planning team that the small tools are useful, but our weekly calls still need a person to decide. Our company pays me to own the missed deadlines, not to admire a tidy chart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm underpaid for leading eight people, and my MBA loan leaves me with less than a month of bills saved. If nothing big changes, that squeeze stays; a little automation won't earn me a raise by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this Friday, I'll keep using AI to draft the supplier summary, then check every number before the Monday meeting. In the first year of this plateau, I'll make an extra 100 payment from each paycheck toward the loan and ask my director for a pay review after the next delivery cycle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady about the work and irritated about the money. My rent goes up faster than the company moves on pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show your director at that pay review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the last four delivery reports and mark where my team caught a late order before it hit a customer. My director can argue with the number, but not with the orders we saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the pay review goes nowhere, do you leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not over one no; there are few comparable manager roles near my home. I'd first ask for a date and a target, because an empty promise does nothing for my loan.

say: I'd say **small tools** help with supplier reports, while managers still own late orders.
I'd tell my team **weekly decisions** still need a person who knows the customers.
think: My **MBA loan** and low manager pay keep my savings below one month of bills.
A small time saving won't become a **raise** unless I make the case myself.
do: Check **AI summaries** against supplier numbers before each Monday meeting.
Pay an **extra 100 per paycheck** toward my loan and request a pay review after the next delivery cycle.
feel: I feel **steady** about work, but irritated by rent and pay.
S0.quote: Our company pays me to own the missed deadlines, not to admire a tidy chart.
fieldNote: Her **work confidence** is real, while the loan and rising rent keep her monthly budget tight.
She treats a pay review as a **measured negotiation**, not an excuse to walk away from scarce local roles.

steps.text: Check AI supplier summaries against source numbers each Monday
Make an extra 100 MBA loan payment from each paycheck

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should test the new buying and planning systems on one team before rolling them out everywhere. I'd also say people who spot a bad order or calm a furious customer still earn their place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know the company may decide one manager can supervise what two used to do. I use AI every day, but being quick with a tool doesn't mean the director keeps my salary line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll map how our eight people spend their hours and learn the new planning system before procurement picks a vendor. During the first year of steady disruption, I'd volunteer to lead the rollout, keep the customer exceptions in our team, and save another 200 a month if my pay allows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm excited by a cleaner process and anxious about the headcount meeting. I can picture my name on both the rollout plan and the cut list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which work would you refuse to hand over without a person checking it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Supplier substitutions need a human call when the customer has a fixed installation date. A wrong delivery can strand a crew, and the software won't stand in front of the customer that morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound keen to lead it, but you fear cuts. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leading is the best chance I see to stay useful, not a guarantee. I won't tell my team their jobs are safe just because I got the project.

say: I'd back a **one-team test** before the company changes buying and planning across every department.
I'd say **customer exceptions** still need a person who can make a call and answer for it.
think: One manager may soon cover **two teams**, putting my own salary at risk.
Daily AI use helps me compete, but it doesn't guarantee my **manager role** survives.
do: Map my team's **eight workloads** this month and learn the new planning system before vendor selection.
Lead the **first-year rollout** if chosen, keeping customer exceptions with people and saving 200 monthly when possible.
feel: I feel **excited** by better planning and anxious about the headcount meeting.
S1.quote: I can picture my name on both the rollout plan and the cut list.
fieldNote: Her **public test-first line** is measured; privately, she expects management posts to be combined.
She sees rollout leadership as a **chance**, and refuses to use it as false reassurance for her team.

steps.text: Learn the new planning system before procurement selects a vendor
Save another 200 monthly if manager pay permits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team that AGI by 2028 means we document decisions and demand an honest staffing plan now. I wouldn't pretend a cheaper system that can do nearly all our planning leaves eight desks and my manager chair untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking part is nearly my whole job, from allocation plans to checking performance reports; robots in 2031 barely change my risk. My loan and thin savings mean a lost salary in 2028 could put me behind on rent within weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'd ask my director for a written timeline and use today's AI to record where our plans fail, while saving up to 300 a month when pay allows. In the first year after 2028, I'd trial AGI with real error checks; if my post is cut, I'd apply to operations lead jobs outside this town and take contract process work only after securing a written fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm frightened, and I don't have the luxury of acting helpless. Two years is one budget cycle and a bit, not enough to build six months of savings from my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you ask for in that staffing plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask which teams will be combined, when the decision is made, and what severance looks like. I won't trade my team's trust for a vague promise of redeployment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take contract work despite the uncertainty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with the fee and payment date on paper. My rent can't wait for a client's good intentions. I'd ask my older sister to let me stay for a month if I lost the job before a contract paid; our family has always lent a room before lending money.

say: I'd ask for a **written staffing plan** before AGI changes how our company allocates work.
I'd tell my team the **manager chair** may disappear along with planning desks.
think: My **thinking work** is exposed in 2028; the later robot date offers little shelter.
With less than one month saved, losing pay could make **rent** late within weeks.
do: Request the **staffing timeline** tomorrow and use current AI to log planning errors.
Save up to **300 monthly** when pay allows; seek outside operations posts if cut after 2028.
feel: I feel **frightened**, but determined to act before the next budget decision.
S2.quote: My rent can't wait for a client's good intentions.
fieldNote: She locates the risk in **2028 thinking work**, correctly separating it from robots expected in 2031.
Her thin cushion makes a **written payment date** essential before she accepts contract work.

steps.text: Use current AI to log plan errors, then trial AGI after 2028
Save up to 300 monthly when pay allows
Apply for operations lead posts outside town if cut after 2028
Ask older sister for housing if job ends before a contract pays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 gives our company time to say which management jobs remain and train people for those jobs. I'd want the directors to publish milestones instead of announcing a finished decision at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me pay down the MBA loan and grow a real cash reserve, though the planning and reporting parts of my job still face the 2031 system. Robots arriving around 2034 don't buy a desk manager extra time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Beginning next quarter, I'd put 150 a month into cash and take a course in contract negotiation, where judging a dispute might still need a named person. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd seek a role managing supplier disputes if the company keeps one, or apply for those roles in the next city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alert rather than cornered. I can make five years count, but I can't save my way out of every possible cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why contract negotiation rather than another AI course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already use AI daily and can learn a new interface in a week. The hard part is deciding what concession a supplier can actually honor, then looking a customer in the eye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company froze raises while giving me two teams, I'd start interviewing before they made that arrangement permanent. A promotion in name alone won't pay my loan.

say: I'd press directors for **staffing milestones** and training plans before 2031.
I'd tell colleagues five years gives us time to seek **named roles**, not just vague promises.
think: Paying down the **MBA loan** and building cash would make a 2031 cut less immediate.
Robots in 2034 offer little relief because **planning and reports** are my main work.
do: Set aside **150 monthly** next quarter and study contract negotiation.
Seek **supplier dispute** management work after 2031, in this company or the next city.
feel: I feel **alert** with time to prepare, though still worried about cuts.
S3.quote: A promotion in name alone won't pay my loan.
fieldNote: She uses the extra **three years** to build cash and shift toward disputes, not to ignore exposure.
Her appetite for new tools remains high; she puts training time into **commercial judgment** instead.

steps.text: Put 150 monthly into cash starting next quarter
Take a contract negotiation course before 2031
Apply for next-city supplier dispute roles if no company role remains after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger staff that AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to choose different work, not a decade to wait. I'd ask the company to show each year's changes so people can plan families and careers honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 27, I'd be 37 when the thinking system arrives, and I could have a different career by then if I work at it. My worry is getting comfortable in this chair while the company quietly stops developing managers; robots around 2039 aren't the danger to my desk work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep my team on the current delivery targets and start saving 150 a month, then look for a better-paid operations post next spring. Over the decade I'd build experience in supplier relationships; in the first year after 2036, I'd review whether my role still needs me before changing jobs again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel hopeful about the time and wary of wasting it. Ten years is enough to build choices if I actually make the moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why chase a better-paid post next spring instead of waiting here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My thin savings won't grow on promises, and a larger salary would let me clear the loan faster. I'm willing to commute for a job with real responsibility, though I won't move on an uncertain offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you in 2036 that your role still has a purpose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for whether I am still settling real supplier disputes and teaching people, rather than signing off an AI plan unread. A title alone isn't proof that my work matters.

say: I'd tell staff a **decade** allows real career choices if the company shares yearly plans.
I'd ask the company to make **family planning** possible with honest milestones.
think: I could build a different career by **age 37**, but comfort might leave me stranded.
Quietly ending **manager development** would matter more than keeping my current title for now.
do: Save **150 monthly** this year and keep the team on delivery targets.
Seek a **better-paid operations post** next spring; reassess the role after AGI reaches work in 2036.
feel: I feel **hopeful** about the decade and wary of wasting it.
S4.quote: A title alone isn't proof that my work matters.
fieldNote: The long runway changes her from **defense** to a deliberate salary and experience move.
She still separates **2036 thinking work** from the later 2039 robot arrival, which barely affects her desk role.

steps.text: Keep eight staff focused on current delivery targets this year
Save 150 monthly toward a larger emergency fund
Interview for better-paid operations posts next spring

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my planning work changes in two years and I have almost no cash buffer. A written staffing schedule, real severance terms, and a way to test new systems before jobs are cut would help me plan instead of guess.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets blamed when an automated order fails. My team will be asked to put our names on a decision we may not have been allowed to check.

headlineQuote: My team will be asked to put our names on a decision we may not have been allowed to check.
portrait: At **27**, Wendy leads eight supply planners in a large company and uses AI daily after earning an MBA.
Her **thin savings**, loan and low manager pay make even a stable job feel financially fragile.
She moves quickly toward **testing systems**, but insists people must answer for failed customer orders.
A 2028 cut feels urgent; five or ten years allow **cash building** and a move toward supplier disputes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens her planning role before she can build a meaningful cash buffer.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing schedule**, clear severance and checked trials would let her make a workable plan.
